# Education in Nigeria
Nigeria's education system is structured into primary, secondary, and tertiary levels, with a focus on universal access and national curriculum. Primary education, beginning at age 5, lasts six years and includes core subjects such as Mathematics, English, Religious Knowledge, and indigenous languages. Students must pass a Common Entrance Examination (CEC) to advance to secondary school. The Universal Basic Education (UBE) program, introduced in 1999, mandates nine years of uninterrupted schooling (6 years of primary and 3 years of junior secondary), making education free and compulsory.
Secondary education follows a 6-3-3-4 structure: 6 years of primary, 3 years of Junior Secondary School (JSS), and 3 years of Senior Secondary School (SSS). The curriculum includes core subjects like English, Mathematics, Economics, and Civic Education, with students choosing electives in areas such as Science, Arts, or Business. The Senior Secondary Certificate Examination (SSCE), administered by the West African Examinations Council (WAEC), is the main national exam, with a maximum of nine subjects. A student must achieve a minimum of seven credits to qualify for tertiary education.
Tertiary education in Nigeria comprises public and private universities, polytechnics, and colleges of education. The government has established 153 universities, including 40 federal and 45 state-owned institutions, with 68 private universities. Admission to universities is based on WAEC or National Examinations Council (NECO) results, with a minimum of 24 points required for a bachelor's degree. Students may also gain entry through the Joint Universities Pre-Matriculation Board (JUPEB) or the Interim Joint Matriculation Board (IJMB) for direct entry into the second year of university.
Private schools are common and often more expensive, with fees increasing rapidly (up to 50–70% in 2024). These schools typically offer smaller class sizes, modern equipment, and better learning environments. However, they remain a minority compared to public institutions, which are more accessible due to their free tuition.
Vocational education is managed by the National Board for Technical Education (NBTE) and includes National Technical Certificates (NTC) and Advanced National Technical Certificates (ANTC). The system faces challenges such as outdated curricula, poor infrastructure, and a shortage of qualified instructors. Apprenticeships are encouraged to bridge the gap between education and employment.
The government has made significant efforts to improve literacy and access, especially for girls and rural populations. Female participation in education has increased, though challenges such as early marriage, teen pregnancy, and cultural norms persist. The government has launched initiatives like the Girls' Education Project and the National Literacy Program to address these issues.
Despite progress, Nigeria faces persistent challenges, including teacher shortages, low teacher qualifications, poor infrastructure, and regional disparities. The quality of education remains uneven, with many students relying on private tutoring to supplement classroom learning. The government continues to invest in education, with education spending around 25% of the annual budget, though challenges remain in ensuring equitable access and quality across regions.
